newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU moves closer to clearing BT/MCI merger.
newsitem.headline: EU moves closer to clearing BT/MCI merger.

text.p: The European Commission will clear the merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp of the United States if the firms confirm proposed "remedies to competition problems", European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Monday.

"If they confirm suggestions they have already made, I will be in a position to approve the merger," Van Miert told a conference organised by the University of Leuven, the Belgian news agency Belga reported.
Van Miert's spokesman confirmed the report.

The Commission started a full probe into the $20 billion merger at the end of January saying it was concerned that it might harm fair competition on the route between the U.S and Britain as well as the U.S.-Europe route. It has until June 11 to take a final decision.
British Telecommunications Plc declined to comment on the remedies or even if the two companies had offered any.
"We're discussing with the Commission. The press release of January 30 listed the issues," BT's head of European Union affairs Larry Stone told Reuters.

The Commission said in the January statement that it would investigate further whether the new entity, called Concert Plc, could divert U.S.-European traffic through the UK or whether it would have any impact on the availability of transatlantic cable capacity to new market entrants.
The impact of the merger on the teleconferencing market would also have to be carefully assessed.

Van Miert on Monday singled out transatlantic cable capacity as one of the outstanding problems, according to Belga. His comments on BT/MCI were intended to ilustrate recent developments in the European telecoms market, Bruno Vanneuville, a researcher who participated in the meeting, told Reuters.

The deal, which involves BT taking over MCI, was not expected to pose major competition problems in Europe because the British telecoms sector is more liberalised than any other market in continental Europe.

It faces its most important test in the United States where legislation forbids a foreign company from taking more than a 20 percent stake in a U.S. firm unless its home market is effectively open to competition.
